title: The strict separation rule
blocks: p

This chapter rests on one rule that decides more Lexical Resource marks than any other single habit: informal idioms belong in Speaking, not in Writing Task 2. The same expression that earns you a point in the interview can cost you one in the essay. This is not a small stylistic preference; it is a register rule, and register is exactly what the higher bands test.
p

Here is why the split is so sharp. IELTS Speaking rewards natural, spontaneous language, so a well-placed idiom (it was a blessing in disguise, I was over the moon) signals that you can use English the way a fluent speaker actually does. Writing Task 2, by contrast, is a formal academic essay.
p

In that context an idiom reads as casual, unserious, and out of place, and it pulls your tone down toward Band 6 no matter how impressive the idiom is. The examiner is not asking “does this candidate know idioms.” The examiner is asking “does this candidate know where each kind of language belongs.”
h2
The decision rule
ul
**Safe for Task 2:** Would this sound natural in a newspaper editorial or an academic article? If yes, use it in your essay.
**Keep for Speaking:** Would this sound at home in a friendly chat? If yes, keep it out of Writing Task 2.
note

**Phrasal verbs:** Many are neutral and perfectly fine in writing (carry out, bring about, result in). The informal, idiomatic ones to keep out of Task 2 are get its act together, cough up, and pull your socks up. When in doubt, choose the single formal verb (organise, pay, improve).

title: 50 Speaking idioms (1–25)
blocks: tip
Use these to sound natural in the interview. The Part label shows where each fits best. Do not carry any of them into a Task 2 essay.
h2
Part 1
ul
**once in a blue moon**: very rarely. Example: I eat out once in a blue moon.
**a piece of cake**: very easy. Example: For me, cooking is a piece of cake.
**cost an arm and a leg**: to be very expensive. Example: Concert tickets cost an arm and a leg.
**a stone’s throw away**: very close. Example: My office is a stone’s throw away from home.
**a rip-off**: something overpriced. Example: That cafe is a total rip-off.
**hit it off**: to get along instantly. Example: We hit it off the moment we met.
**call it a day**: to stop working for the day. Example: By six, I usually call it a day.
**get the hang of it**: to learn how to do something. Example: It took me a week to get the hang of it.
**lend a hand**: to help. Example: I often lend a hand at home.
**money doesn’t grow on trees**: money is limited. Example: My parents always said money doesn’t grow on trees.
**hit the books**: to study hard. Example: I need to hit the books this weekend.
h2
Part 2
ul
**over the moon**: extremely happy. Example: I was over the moon when I passed.
**on cloud nine**: blissfully happy. Example: On my wedding day, I was on cloud nine.
**down in the dumps**: sad or low. Example: I felt down in the dumps after the result.
**butterflies in my stomach**: nervous excitement. Example: I had butterflies in my stomach before the interview.
**get cold feet**: to become nervous at the last minute. Example: I nearly got cold feet before the speech.
**a fish out of water**: uncomfortable in a new setting. Example: On my first day abroad, I felt like a fish out of water.
**the last straw**: the final thing one can tolerate. Example: The delay was the last straw.
**a blessing in disguise**: a hidden benefit in a setback. Example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
**the icing on the cake**: a welcome extra bonus. Example: The view was the icing on the cake.
**in at the deep end**: thrown into something difficult with no preparation. Example: I was thrown in at the deep end on day one.
**burn the midnight oil**: to work or study late into the night. Example: Before finals, I burn the midnight oil.
h2
Part 3
ul
**go the extra mile**: to make a special effort. Example: Good teachers go the extra mile.
**pull your socks up**: to improve your effort. Example: I had to pull my socks up after the mock test.
**get the ball rolling**: to start something. Example: Let me get the ball rolling on the project.

title: 50 Speaking idioms (26–50)
blocks: h2
Part 3
ul
**get to grips with**: to begin to understand or manage. Example: It takes time to get to grips with a new city.
**a foot in the door**: an initial opportunity. Example: An internship gets your foot in the door.
**spread your wings**: to become independent and try new things. Example: University lets young people spread their wings.
**keep up with the times**: to stay current. Example: Businesses must keep up with the times.
**hit the nail on the head**: to say exactly the right thing. Example: You’ve hit the nail on the head.
**see the bigger picture**: to grasp the whole situation. Example: Leaders must see the bigger picture.
**think outside the box**: to think creatively. Example: Innovation means thinking outside the box.
**keep an open mind**: to stay receptive to new ideas. Example: It helps to keep an open mind.
**sit on the fence**: to avoid taking a side. Example: On this issue, I refuse to sit on the fence.
**a mixed blessing**: something with both good and bad sides. Example: Social media is a mixed blessing.
**the best of both worlds**: two benefits at once. Example: Remote work offers the best of both worlds.
**every cloud has a silver lining**: good can come from bad. Example: Every cloud has a silver lining.
**on the same wavelength**: sharing the same thinking. Example: My colleague and I are on the same wavelength.
**in the same boat**: in the same difficult situation. Example: During the crisis, we were all in the same boat.
**kill two birds with one stone**: to solve two things at once. Example: Cycling to work kills two birds with one stone.
**at the drop of a hat**: instantly, without hesitation. Example: She would travel at the drop of a hat.
**add fuel to the fire**: to make a bad situation worse. Example: His comment only added fuel to the fire.
**a needle in a haystack**: nearly impossible to find. Example: Finding a quiet flat there is like finding a needle in a haystack.
**pull strings**: to use influence to get something. Example: He pulled strings to get the job.
**face the music**: to accept the consequences. Example: Sooner or later, you have to face the music.
**bite off more than you can chew**: to take on too much. Example: I bit off more than I could chew last term.
h2
Part 2
ul
**learn something the hard way**: to learn through difficult experience. Example: I learned time management the hard way.
**in the middle of nowhere**: in a very remote place. Example: The resort was in the middle of nowhere.
**a change of scenery**: a refreshing change of place. Example: A holiday gives you a change of scenery.
**the trip of a lifetime**: an unforgettable journey. Example: Visiting the mountains was the trip of a lifetime.

title: 50 Writing collocations (1–25)
blocks: tip
Use these in Writing Task 2. Every one is formal and essay-appropriate.
h2
Introducing and framing
ul
**it is widely acknowledged that**: many accept as true. Example: It is widely acknowledged that education reduces poverty.
**there is no denying that**: it cannot be denied. Example: There is no denying that technology has reshaped work.
**a growing body of evidence suggests that**: increasing research indicates. Example: A growing body of evidence suggests that pollution harms cognition.
**it can be argued that**: one could reasonably claim. Example: It can be argued that fees limit access.
**this essay will examine both views**: signals a balanced essay. Example: This essay will examine both views before offering an opinion.
**a widely held view**: a common opinion. Example: A widely held view is that competition improves standards.
h2
Building an argument
ul
**it stands to reason that**: it is logical that. Example: It stands to reason that better roads reduce delays.
**a compelling argument**: a convincing case. Example: There is a compelling argument for renewable subsidies.
**a valid point**: a reasonable claim. Example: Opponents make a valid point about cost.
**proponents argue that**: supporters claim. Example: Proponents argue that automation raises productivity.
**critics contend that**: opponents assert. Example: Critics contend that it destroys jobs.
**it is worth noting that**: a point deserves attention. Example: It is worth noting that results vary by region.
h2
Cause and effect
ul
**play a pivotal role in**: to be centrally important. Example: Education plays a pivotal role in development.
**give rise to**: to cause. Example: Rapid growth gives rise to inequality.
**stem from**: to originate in. Example: Many problems stem from poverty.
**be attributed to**: to be explained by. Example: The decline can be attributed to weak demand.
**a contributing factor**: one of several causes. Example: Poor diet is a contributing factor in obesity.
**have far-reaching consequences**: to have wide effects. Example: Climate change has far-reaching consequences.
**as a direct result of**: caused straightforwardly by. Example: As a direct result of the ban, sales fell.
h2
Contrast and concession
ul
**while it is true that**: conceding a point. Example: While it is true that costs are high, benefits outweigh them.
**contrary to popular belief**: against common opinion. Example: Contrary to popular belief, remote work can raise output.
**despite the fact that**: introduces a full concession clause. Example: Despite the fact that it is costly, the plan is justified.
**on the one hand … on the other hand**: balancing two sides. Example: On the one hand it saves time; on the other, it isolates people.
**to a certain extent**: partly. Example: This is true to a certain extent.
h2
Solutions and evaluation
ul
**address the issue**: to deal with a problem. Example: Governments must address the issue urgently.

title: 50 Writing collocations (26–50)
blocks: h2
Solutions and evaluation
ul
**tackle the root cause**: to deal with the underlying reason. Example: Lasting change means tackling the root cause.
**implement effective measures**: to put good policies in place. Example: Cities should implement effective measures against pollution.
**a viable solution**: a workable answer. Example: Public transport is a viable solution to congestion.
**weigh the pros and cons**: to consider both sides. Example: Policymakers must weigh the pros and cons.
**strike a balance between**: to find a fair middle. Example: We must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
**take into account**: to consider. Example: Any policy must take into account rural needs.
h2
Degree, scale, and time
ul
**a significant proportion of**: a notable share. Example: A significant proportion of graduates work abroad.
**the vast majority of**: almost all. Example: The vast majority of commuters use trains.
**in the long run**: over time. Example: In the long run, prevention is cheaper.
**in the short term**: soon, briefly. Example: In the short term, costs may rise.
**an integral part of**: an essential component. Example: Art is an integral part of education.
**gain momentum**: to grow in strength. Example: The movement has gained momentum.
h2
Impact and trade-off
ul
**pose a serious threat to**: to endanger. Example: Rising seas pose a serious threat to coasts.
**have a detrimental effect on**: to harm. Example: Stress has a detrimental effect on health.
**reap the benefits of**: to enjoy the rewards. Example: Future generations will reap the benefits of this investment.
**at the expense of**: sacrificing something else. Example: Growth should not come at the expense of the environment.
h2
Examples and emphasis
ul
**a case in point**: a fitting example. Example: Singapore is a case in point.
**to illustrate this**: to give an example. Example: To illustrate this, consider public transport in Tokyo.
**bear in mind that**: to remember. Example: We must bear in mind that resources are finite.
**shed light on**: to clarify. Example: The study sheds light on the causes.
**in light of**: considering. Example: In light of these findings, reform is needed.
h2
Stance and conclusion
ul
**from my perspective**: in my opinion. Example: From my perspective, the benefits outweigh the risks.
**more often than not**: usually. Example: More often than not, early action is cheaper.
**by and large**: generally. Example: By and large, the policy has succeeded.
**draw a firm conclusion**: to reach a clear judgement. Example: It is difficult to draw a firm conclusion from limited data.

title: Practice · Register sort and idiom repair
blocks: exercise

blocks.title: Exercise 5.1 · Register and Style Sort
blocks.instructions: Each sentence below is written as if it appeared in a Writing Task 2 essay. Decide whether the underlined language is appropriate for a formal essay (mark it W) or belongs only in Speaking (mark it S). For every S, rewrite the sentence in formal academic English suitable for Task 2.

items.prompt: Nowadays, a lot of kids are glued to their phones around the clock.
items.answer: S — These days, many children spend excessive time on their smartphones.
items.reason: A lot of kids, glued to, around the clock are all informal.

items.prompt: It is widely acknowledged that education reduces poverty.
The government needs to get its act together on pollution.
items.answer: S — The government must take decisive action on pollution.
items.reason: Get its act together is informal.

items.prompt: This policy could have far-reaching consequences.
At the end of the day, it is up to the individual.
items.answer: S — Ultimately, the responsibility lies with the individual.
items.reason: At the end of the day, it is up to are informal.

items.prompt: Renewable energy plays a pivotal role in cutting emissions.
Fast food is a rip-off and bad for you.
items.answer: S — Fast food is both overpriced and detrimental to health.
items.reason: A rip-off, bad for you are informal.

items.prompt: There is no denying that technology has transformed education.
Loads of people reckon that exams are unfair.
items.answer: S — A significant proportion of people believe that exams are unfair.

items.prompt: Poverty can be attributed to a range of social factors.
Young people these days could not care less about tradition.
items.answer: S — Many young people today show little interest in tradition.
items.reason: Could not care less is informal.

items.prompt: Governments must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
Social media is a double-edged sword, to be honest.
items.answer: S — Social media brings both clear benefits and serious drawbacks.
items.reason: To be honest is a spoken hedge.

items.prompt: This crisis stems from decades of underinvestment.
If you ask me, the whole system is a mess.
items.answer: S — In my view, the current system is deeply flawed.
items.reason: If you ask me, a mess are informal.

items.prompt: A growing body of evidence suggests a link between diet and disease.
Tourism can boost the economy, but it is a bit of a mixed bag.
items.answer: S — Tourism can boost the economy, though it brings mixed outcomes.
items.reason: A bit of a mixed bag is informal.

items.prompt: In the long run, prevention is cheaper than treatment.
The rich should cough up more tax.
items.answer: S — The wealthy should contribute more in taxes.

items.prompt: It is worth noting that not all solutions are equally effective.

blocks: note

**Why:** informal idioms and phrasal verbs lower the register of a Task 2 essay, which pulls Lexical Resource down even when the vocabulary is otherwise rich. The formal rewrites preserve the meaning while restoring academic tone.
exercise

blocks.title: Exercise 5.2 · Idiom Substitution
blocks.instructions: Each Speaking response below contains an idiom that is misremembered, misused, or wrong. Rewrite the underlined part with the correct, natural form. Type the correct idiom.

items.prompt: When I got the scholarship, I was on cloud seven.
The final test was a piece of pie for me.
On my first day abroad, I felt like a fish in the water.
items.reason: Not “a fish in the water”; it means uncomfortable in a new situation.

items.prompt: My university is just a stone throw from my house.
Learning to drive was a really steep hill at first.
We managed to kill two birds in one stone by cycling to work.
items.answer: kill two birds with one stone

items.prompt: After the experiment failed, it was back to the painting board.
Honestly, I would travel at the drop of the hat.
items.answer: at the drop of a hat
